CARDIAC INVESTIGATIONS__Exercise Toleran:
The exercise tolerance test (ETT), or exercise ECG, records a 12-lead ECG and blood pressure while the patient exercises on a treadmill against a progressively increasing workload. It looks for inducible myocardial ischaemia, quantifies exercise capacity, and helps with risk stratification in known or suspected coronary artery disease. NICE now prefers CT coronary angiography for diagnosing stable angina, but the ETT retains a role in functional and rhythm assessment.

1Indication & principle

Progressive treadmill exercise raises heart rate, contractility and afterload, increasing myocardial oxygen demand. A flow-limiting coronary stenosis cannot augment supply to match demand, producing demand ischaemia that manifests as ST-segment changes, symptoms, arrhythmia or an abnormal blood-pressure response.

Detecting inducible ischaemia in suspected or known stable coronary disease.
Assessing exercise capacity and provoking exertional symptoms or arrhythmia.
Risk stratification after MI or in established disease (e.g. left main / triple-vessel clues).
2How it is performed

A continuous 12-lead ECG and periodic BP are recorded at rest and throughout graded exercise, most commonly using the Bruce protocol, which increases treadmill speed and incline every 3 minutes. The aim is to reach a target heart rate (roughly 85% of the age-predicted maximum, i.e. 220 − age) unless a symptom or ECG endpoint stops the test first. Recording continues into recovery, as ST changes may appear or persist post-exercise.

Preparation: withhold rate-limiting drugs (e.g. beta-blockers) if diagnostic testing is intended and safe; suitable footwear; informed consent.
Resuscitation facilities and trained staff must be immediately available.
3Interpretation

A test is positive when exercise induces ischaemic ST-segment depression; other findings point to severity or make the test non-diagnostic.

Horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥ 1 mm→Inducible myocardial ischaemia (positive test)
ST elevation in non-infarct (non-Q) leads→Severe transmural ischaemia — stop immediately
Fall in systolic BP or failure to rise on exertion→Severe disease (e.g. left main / triple-vessel) — stop test
Target heart rate not reached, no symptoms/ECG change→Non-diagnostic (submaximal) test
4Pitfalls, limitations & contraindications

The resting ECG must be interpretable: pre-existing LBBB, ventricular pacing, WPW, LVH with strain or digoxin effect render ST analysis unreliable. Sensitivity and specificity are modest, so false positives (especially in women and low pre-test probability) and false negatives occur. Patients unable to exercise adequately need pharmacological or imaging alternatives.

🚫Acute MI / unstable angina
Absolute contraindication — risk of infarction or arrest
💔Severe aortic stenosis
Symptomatic severe AS — risk of syncope / sudden death
⚡Uncontrolled arrhythmia
Haemodynamically significant rhythm disturbance
🩸Uncontrolled hypertension
Severe uncontrolled BP is a relative contraindication
🚩 STOP the test immediately for a fall in systolic BP, ST elevation, chest pain with significant ST depression, a serious arrhythmia, or the patient becoming distressed. Exertional hypotension is an ominous sign suggesting severe or left main disease. The ETT is contraindicated in unstable angina and in severe symptomatic aortic stenosis.
🎓 ≥ 1 mm of horizontal or downsloping ST depression = a positive test. Exertional hypotension is an ominous marker of severe (e.g. left main / triple-vessel) disease. Remember NICE now prefers CT coronary angiography for diagnosing stable angina.
CARDIAC INVESTIGATIONS__24h Holter / Eve:
A 24-hour (ambulatory) Holter monitor is a portable device that records a continuous ECG while the patient goes about normal daily life, allowing intermittent cardiac rhythm disturbances to be captured and correlated with symptoms via a patient-kept diary. Its central purpose is to answer one question: are this patient's palpitations, dizziness or blackouts caused by an arrhythmia? Longer recordings (48–72h Holter, patient-activated external event/loop recorders, or an implantable loop recorder) extend the monitoring window when symptoms are infrequent.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to investigate intermittent symptoms that a resting 12-lead ECG (a single snapshot) is likely to miss. The principle is symptom–rhythm correlation: prolonged continuous recording increases the chance of catching a transient event and timestamping it against the patient's diary.

Palpitations — document paroxysmal AF, SVT or ventricular ectopy/VT.
Unexplained syncope / presyncope — look for pauses, high-grade AV block or bradyarrhythmia.
Known/suspected paroxysmal AF — detect and quantify AF burden.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Chest electrodes connect to a small recorder worn for 24–72 hours. The patient continues usual activities and, crucially, keeps a symptom diary noting the time and nature of every symptom (palpitation, dizziness, blackout). Skin is kept dry; some devices must be removed for bathing. On return, the recording is analysed and diary times are cross-referenced against the trace. Match the device to symptom frequency:

🧪24–72h Holter
Daily or near-daily symptoms
🧪External event / loop recorder
Weekly-to-monthly symptoms; worn for weeks
🧪Implantable loop recorder
Rare (e.g. < monthly) but serious episodes; up to ~3 years
3INTERPRETATION

Interpretation hinges on lining up the diary timestamp with the simultaneous rhythm:

Symptomatic palpitations coinciding with a captured arrhythmia (paroxysmal AF, SVT, VT)→Arrhythmia confirmed as the cause of symptoms
Symptoms occurring with a NORMAL sinus rhythm on the trace→Symptoms are not arrhythmic — rules arrhythmia out for that episode
Infrequent (e.g. monthly) symptoms with no event during a 24h recording→24h Holter likely to miss them — use a prolonged event/loop recorder
Syncope with a documented pause or complete (third-degree) heart block→Permanent pacemaker indicated
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Sampling window: a normal 24h trace only reflects the day(s) recorded — it cannot exclude an arrhythmia the patient did not have during monitoring.
Diary dependence: if the patient forgets to log symptoms, correlation is lost and the study is often non-diagnostic.
Asymptomatic findings: incidental ectopy or brief runs without symptoms may be over-interpreted.
🚩 A normal 24-hour Holter does NOT exclude a paroxysmal arrhythmia when symptoms are infrequent — match monitor duration to symptom frequency and escalate to prolonged external or implantable loop recorders. Unexplained syncope with structural heart disease or a high-risk ECG needs urgent specialist assessment, not merely outpatient monitoring.
🎓 Match the monitor duration to how often symptoms occur. The diary correlating symptoms to rhythm is the key output — capturing a NORMAL rhythm during symptoms is just as diagnostically useful as capturing an arrhythmia, because it redirects the workup away from the heart.
CARDIAC INVESTIGATIONS__Coronary Angiogr:
Coronary angiography is the invasive gold-standard for defining coronary artery anatomy and quantifying stenosis. A catheter is advanced to the coronary ostia and iodinated contrast is injected under fluoroscopy to opacify the lumen, allowing narrowings to be identified, functionally assessed, and often treated by PCI in the same sitting.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

It is the definitive test for coronary anatomy, used when the result will change management. Contrast fills the coronary lumen so that stenoses appear as luminal narrowings on the fluoroscopic image, and lesions can be treated in the same procedure.

Acute coronary syndrome — immediate angiography for primary PCI in STEMI, and early invasive assessment in high-risk NSTEMI/unstable angina.
Stable angina — high-risk patients or ongoing symptoms despite optimal medical therapy.
Pre-operative — before valve or other cardiac surgery to define coronary disease.
Inconclusive non-invasive tests — when CT coronary angiography or functional imaging is equivocal.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Performed awake under local anaesthetic with continuous ECG and haemodynamic monitoring. The radial artery is the preferred (first-line) access; the femoral artery is an alternative. A sheath is placed, catheters are advanced retrogradely to the left and right coronary ostia, and contrast is hand-injected in multiple projections.

Patient preparation: consent, check renal function and clotting, and give dual antiplatelet therapy if PCI is anticipated.
FFR (fractional flow reserve) uses a pressure wire during adenosine-induced hyperaemia to assess the functional significance of intermediate lesions.
Post-procedure: radial band or femoral haemostasis, and monitoring of the access site for bleeding.
3INTERPRETATION

Stenoses are graded by percentage luminal narrowing of the major epicardial vessels, with FFR resolving borderline cases. The pattern of disease guides whether PCI or CABG is preferred.

≥70% of a major epicardial vessel, or ≥50% left main→Significant flow-limiting stenosis — consider revascularisation (PCI or CABG)
FFR ≤0.80 across a lesion→Functionally significant — revascularise
Left main or triple-vessel disease→Often favours CABG over PCI — discuss at heart team
Normal coronaries with angina→Consider microvascular angina or a non-cardiac cause
🧪LAD
Left anterior descending — supplies the anterior wall and septum
🧪Circumflex
Supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle
🧪RCA
Right coronary — supplies the inferior wall and often the AV node
🧪Left main
Feeds LAD and circumflex — ≥50% stenosis is significant and high-risk
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

Angiography images the lumen only and can underestimate diffuse disease or plaque burden; intermediate lesions may look significant but be functionally trivial, which is why FFR is used. It is invasive and carries real risk, so it should be reserved for when the findings will alter management.

Contrast nephropathy is a concern in renal impairment — hydrate and minimise contrast volume.
Iodinated contrast allergy must be checked beforehand.
🚩 Procedural risks include access-site bleeding/haematoma and arterial injury, stroke, MI, arrhythmia, contrast nephropathy (hydrate; take care in renal impairment) and contrast allergy. It is invasive — reserve it for when the result will change management, and use the radial route to reduce bleeding complications.
🎓 Radial access is first-line and reduces bleeding versus femoral. A stenosis is significant at ≥70% of an epicardial vessel or ≥50% of the left main; FFR ≤0.80 defines a functionally significant lesion; and left main or triple-vessel disease often favours CABG.
CARDIAC INVESTIGATIONS__Tilt Table Test:
The tilt table test (head-up tilt test) is a provocative bedside autonomic investigation used to evaluate recurrent unexplained syncope. The patient is secured to a motorised table and tilted head-up for a prolonged period while heart rate and blood pressure are monitored continuously; sustained upright posture provokes the abnormal autonomic reflex, allowing the underlying mechanism — vasovagal (reflex) syncope, orthostatic hypotension or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (PoTS) — to be reproduced and identified.

1Indication & principle
Investigation of recurrent unexplained syncope where a reflex (vasovagal) or orthostatic cause is suspected and initial assessment (history, examination, lying/standing BP, 12-lead ECG) is non-diagnostic.
Also useful in suspected PoTS and to distinguish true syncope from psychogenic pseudosyncope.
Principle: prolonged head-up posture causes venous pooling in the lower limbs, reducing venous return and stroke volume. In susceptible individuals this triggers an exaggerated autonomic reflex — paradoxical vasodilatation and/or bradycardia (the Bezold–Jarisch response) — that reproduces the patient's spontaneous faint under controlled, monitored conditions.
2How it is performed
Preparation: patient fasted, supine on a motorised table with a footplate and safety straps. Continuous ECG and beat-to-beat (or frequent non-invasive) blood pressure monitoring; IV access and resuscitation equipment available.
Baseline: rest supine for ~5–10 minutes to establish stable heart rate and BP.
Tilt phase: table raised to 60–70° head-up and held for a prolonged period (typically 20–45 minutes) while symptoms and haemodynamics are watched.
Provocation (optional): if the passive phase is negative, sublingual GTN (or IV isoprenaline) may be given to increase sensitivity. The endpoint is reproduction of the patient's symptoms or completion of the protocol; the table is then rapidly returned to supine.
3Interpretation
Gradual or sudden fall in BP with bradycardia, reproducing syncope→Vasovagal (neurally-mediated reflex) syncope
Sustained fall in systolic BP ≥20 mmHg on tilting without adequate compensatory tachycardia→Orthostatic hypotension (autonomic failure, drugs, hypovolaemia)
Marked rise in heart rate >30 bpm with symptoms but no hypotension→Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (PoTS)
Normal heart rate and BP maintained throughout, no symptoms→Negative test — seek a cardiac or other cause
🧪Vasovagal
Hypotension + bradycardia reproducing the faint
💧Orthostatic
Systolic BP drop ≥20 mmHg, blunted tachycardia
💓PoTS
HR rise >30 bpm, symptoms, BP maintained
✅Negative
Stable haemodynamics — look elsewhere
4Pitfalls & limitations
Imperfect sensitivity/specificity: a negative test does not exclude reflex syncope, and false positives occur in asymptomatic people, so results must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture.
Reproducibility is only moderate; symptom reproduction is the most meaningful endpoint.
Provocative agents (GTN, isoprenaline) raise sensitivity but reduce specificity. The test is time-consuming and requires trained staff and continuous monitoring.
🚩 Exclude a cardiac cause of syncope FIRST. Structural heart disease and arrhythmia (complete heart block, VT, long QT) are dangerous and must be ruled out before attributing syncope to a benign reflex cause. Red-flag syncope — exertional or lying-down onset, associated palpitations, family history of sudden death, or an abnormal ECG — mandates cardiac work-up, NOT a tilt test.
🎓 The tilt table test diagnoses vasovagal syncope, orthostatic hypotension and PoTS by reproducing symptoms under controlled tilt. Always exclude arrhythmic/structural cardiac syncope first — it is the life-threatening cause.
CARDIAC INVESTIGATIONS__Electrophysiolog:
An electrophysiology (EP) study is an invasive procedure in which electrode catheters are advanced transvenously into the heart to record intracardiac electrograms and deliver programmed electrical stimulation. It defines the mechanism of an arrhythmia, risk-stratifies and maps circuits before catheter ablation, and evaluates selected cases of unexplained syncope or conduction disease – and in the same sitting the culprit accessory pathway or re-entry circuit can often be ablated, making it a combined diagnostic and curative tool.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The EP study answers two questions: what is the arrhythmia mechanism, and can it be treated with ablation. Programmed electrical stimulation (timed extra-stimuli and burst pacing) is used to induce a tachycardia, then intracardiac recordings localise the circuit.

Characterise a narrow-complex tachycardia (SVT) – distinguish AVNRT, AVRT (accessory pathway/WPW) and atrial tachycardia.
Map and risk-stratify before catheter ablation of an accessory pathway or re-entry circuit.
Assess ventricular tachycardia substrate in structural heart disease.
Evaluate unexplained syncope or conduction disease when non-invasive tests are inconclusive.
🧪Recording catheters
Sample intracardiac electrograms (HRA, His, coronary sinus, RV)
⚡Programmed stimulation
Extra-stimuli/burst pacing to induce & localise the circuit
🔥Ablation energy
Radiofrequency or cryo destroys the pathway/focus
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Performed in a catheter lab under local anaesthesia and conscious sedation, usually via femoral venous access. Multipolar catheters are positioned under fluoroscopy at key sites; baseline conduction intervals are measured, then pacing manoeuvres attempt to induce the clinical arrhythmia.

Anticoagulation and antiarrhythmic drugs are often withheld beforehand so the arrhythmia remains inducible; consent covers ablation in the same sitting.
Catheters record from high right atrium, His bundle, coronary sinus and right ventricle to build the activation sequence.
Once mapped, radiofrequency (heat) or cryoablation (freezing) is delivered to the target; success is confirmed by non-inducibility.
3INTERPRETATION

Findings guide whether the arrhythmia is ablatable, whether a device is needed, and how much arrhythmic risk the patient carries.

Inducible re-entrant SVT with an accessory pathway (AVNRT, AVRT/WPW)→Map and ablate the pathway – often curative
Inducible sustained VT in structural heart disease→Substrate for ventricular arrhythmia – consider ICD ± ablation
Accessory pathway with short refractory period in WPW + AF→High risk of rapid conduction to VF – ablate
No inducible arrhythmia→Lower arrhythmic risk – reassure/conservative management
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A negative study (non-inducible) does not fully exclude a clinical arrhythmia – sensitivity is imperfect, especially for some VTs.
Sedation, antiarrhythmic drugs and autonomic tone can suppress inducibility and give false-negative results.
It is invasive and resource-intensive, so it is reserved for when ablation or a definitive rhythm diagnosis will change management.
🚩 EP study/ablation carries real procedural risk: cardiac perforation and tamponade, complete heart block (needing a permanent pacemaker – especially with septal pathways near the AV node), vascular access complications, and thromboembolism/stroke. It is invasive and reserved for when ablation or definitive rhythm diagnosis is genuinely needed.
🎓 The EP study is unique in that it both diagnoses the arrhythmia mechanism and enables curative catheter ablation of accessory pathways and re-entry circuits – but ablation adjacent to the AV node risks complete heart block requiring pacing.
CARDIAC INVESTIGATIONS__Endomyocardial B:
Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is a specialised, relatively rarely used invasive test in which small samples of heart muscle are taken transvenously for histological analysis. Its two main roles are surveillance for rejection after cardiac transplantation and diagnosis of specific myocardial diseases — notably suspected myocarditis (especially giant-cell or fulminant disease with haemodynamic compromise or arrhythmia) and infiltrative or storage disorders such as cardiac amyloidosis and sarcoidosis when non-invasive tests are inconclusive.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

EMB is reserved for situations where tissue histology changes management and non-invasive tests fall short. The principle is direct sampling of myocardium so that the microscopic pattern of injury — inflammation, cellular infiltrate, or abnormal deposits — can be identified.

Post-transplant rejection surveillance (the single commonest indication).
Suspected giant-cell or fulminant myocarditis with arrhythmia or haemodynamic compromise.
Infiltrative/storage disease — cardiac amyloidosis or sarcoidosis — when echo, MRI and other tests are inconclusive.
🫀Transplant rejection
Routine surveillance and work-up of suspected acute rejection
🔬Giant-cell myocarditis
Fulminant course, needs aggressive immunosuppression
🧬Amyloidosis
Congo red apple-green birefringence confirms deposits
🟢Sarcoidosis
Non-caseating granulomas on histology
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A flexible cutting catheter called a bioptome is introduced through a central vein — most commonly the right internal jugular vein — and advanced to the right ventricular side of the interventricular septum under fluoroscopic or echocardiographic guidance.

Performed under local anaesthetic with continuous ECG and haemodynamic monitoring.
The septum is targeted (rather than the free wall) to reduce perforation risk.
Several small samples (typically 3–5) are taken and fixed for histology, and where relevant special stains (Congo red) or electron microscopy.
Sampling is inherently patchy because only a few tiny fragments of myocardium are retrieved.
3INTERPRETATION

The histological pattern points to the underlying diagnosis and directs treatment.

Surveillance biopsy: lymphocytic infiltrate + myocyte damage→Acute cellular rejection — escalate immunosuppression
Giant cells with diffuse inflammatory infiltrate→Giant-cell myocarditis — poor prognosis, aggressive immunosuppression
Congo red staining — apple-green birefringence under polarised light→Cardiac amyloidosis
Non-caseating granulomas→Cardiac sarcoidosis
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY

Because myocardial involvement is frequently focal, the bioptome may simply miss affected tissue, so results must always be read alongside the clinical picture and non-invasive imaging.

Sampling error is the key limitation — a negative biopsy does not exclude disease.
Complementary tests (cardiac MRI, bone scintigraphy for amyloid, serum/urine free light chains) help target and interpret biopsy.
Repeat biopsy or additional samples may be needed when suspicion remains high.
🚩 EMB is invasive with a small but serious risk of right ventricular perforation and cardiac tamponade, plus tricuspid valve damage, arrhythmia and heart block. Because myocardial involvement is patchy, sampling error causes false negatives — a negative biopsy does NOT exclude the disease.
🎓 Main uses are transplant rejection surveillance and diagnosing giant-cell myocarditis and infiltrative disease. Remember: amyloid = Congo red apple-green birefringence; sarcoid = non-caseating granulomas. Patchy sampling means a negative result does not exclude disease.
